Speaking earlier today during Hannover Re’s Baden-Baden media briefing, Patrick Horstmann Managing Director, and Head of insurance-linked securities (ILS) at the firm, emphasised that the German reinsurer sees ILS capital as a sustainable addition to the global reinsurance market and a key area of growth for the company.

Hannover Re has been steadily growing in the ILS market in recent years.

In late 2025, the reinsurer launched its Bermuda-based ILS platform, Hannover Re Capital Partners in late 2025, and began writing business at the January 1st 2026 reinsurance renewals to further scale its alternative capital capabilities.

“ILS capital has grown over the last years and has also grown relatively more than traditional reinsurance capital. Meanwhile, it’s roughly 18% of the overall reinsurance capacity, and we see alternative capital as a sustainable addition to the traditional capital in the market,” Horstmann explained during the briefing.

“Especially in the last year we have seen this increase. But we have seen over the long term and over the long horizon the sustainability of ILS capital in the market,” he continued.

Horstmann also outlined that Hannover Re aims to bridge capital markets and cedants, noting that the reinsurer’s ILS activities include five key businesses segments: catastrophe bond transformation, collateralized fronting, life ILS, its cat bond focused manager Leine Investment, and the company’s newest ILS venture the Hannover Re Capital Partners (HCP) unit.

“Since November last year, we have launched an insurance agent in Bermuda called Hannover Re Capital Partners, and that is a platform where we connect third-party capital with the risk, utilising our Hannover Re underwriting, modeling, structuring expertise, and so enabling third-party investors to access traditional reinsurance risk with the help of Hannover Re and the support of Hannover Re,” Horstmann added.

During the Q&A portion, Horstmann provided more detail on HCP.

The executive said the platform is “not a risk-carrying entity” and uses collateralized fronting structures.

He also added that HCP has raised a low triple-digit million amount in assets under management and had fully deployed that capital for the July 1st 2026, renewal.

“At the moment, we are in discussions with further investors to raise additional capital. But I’m always a bit reluctant to give any aims or targets. What I can say is, we are fully aligned with our business plan, which we had initially.

“So we are very satisfied with the development so far and have seen a lot of interest from third-party investors in our activities, appreciating our global market access, our underwriting expertise, and also the ILS knowledge we have gained over the last decades. So we have a lot seen of interest in further discussions,” Horstmann added.

In addition, we also asked Horstmann to outline where Hannover Re sees its biggest opportunities in the capital markets and ILS sector for next year?

“Focusing on the five pillars we have within ILS at Hannover Re, I would say we have a very good market footprint for catastrophe bond transformation and for the collateralized fronting business. So we expect them in the next year, or the next two years, to be stable, potentially slightly growing,” Horstmann said.

Adding: “We have been compared to the market as a bit underrepresented in terms of third-party asset management, so Leine Investment and Hannover Re Capital Partners. So, just because our footprint in the market was not as strong there as for the other areas, I would expect there to be more growth in absolute and on relative terms compared to the other segments.”

We also asked Thorsten Steinmann, CEO, E+S Rück, member of the Executive Board, Hannover Re, whether the reinsurer has any plans in place to look at other opportunities to share risk with investor markets in the near future.

“We’ve always said in the last few weeks because one of those topics which came up is the topic of casualty sidecars, and this is partially done via Lloyd’s partially directly via investors, and this is a space where we are very cautious and we are not playing in this space.

“It’s not part of our product that we are offering to our clients, simply because we believe that the complexity of this long tail business, in combination with the asset management risk that you run, that we are very cautious to play in this field. I’m not saying this is going to be the case forever, but the response today is that we are very cautious and observing,” Steinmann explained.

item.content:encoded:

Franklin Templeton Investment Solutions, the hedge fund-focused arm of the global asset manager, has moderated its stance on the catastrophe bonds asset class slightly from ‘strongly overweight’ to ‘overweight’ for Q4 2026, which in turn has led the firm to shift its stance on the insurance-linked securities market to ‘neutral’.

At the same time, the firm’s neutral stance on other insurance-linked securities (ILS), including private collateralized reinsurance, retrocession, and industry loss warranties (ILWs), remains unchanged.

It’s important to remember that “overweight” on catastrophe bonds remains very positive and means the investment managers continues to see the opportunity in the cat bond asset class as meaningful for portfolios.

Commenting on the cat bond market’s performance in the third quarter of 2026, Franklin Templeton said, “Although there were several notable catastrophe events in August, none resulted in major insured losses affecting the cat bond market. Combined with seasonal factors, cat bond prices stayed strong as the market approached the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season.”

Franklin Templeton also acknowledged that global insured catastrophe losses remained relatively moderate in the first half of 2026, with industry estimates sitting below long-term averages.

The Swiss Re Institute previously estimated that global insured losses from nat cat events reached US $42 billion in the first half of 2026, which the reinsurer said at the time, marked the lowest first-half total recorded since 2020, and 16% below the 10-year average.

In addition, Franklin Templeton noted that several key catastrophe events occurred in August, including earthquakes, floods and wildfires, but stressed that none of these resulted in major insured losses affecting the global cat bond market.

“Atlantic hurricane activity also remained subdued as the season approached its historical peak, broadly consistent with strengthening El Niño conditions. Several tropical storms developed in August, but none intensified into hurricanes. The relatively benign loss environment, seasonal factors and strong investor demand supported cat bond prices and tighter spreads heading into peak hurricane season. While activity has remained subdued, we remain cautious until the season concludes,” Franklin Templeton continued.

“Structurally, we remain constructive on cat bonds, as the market continues to expand, supported by strong investor demand and issuance from both new and returning sponsors. Furthermore, current spreads and yields remain attractive relative to high-yield bonds and the asset class continues to offer low correlation with traditional financial markets.”

Franklin Templeton’s shift on cat bonds is reflected in the firm’s conviction-focused z-score, which has now seen its score decrease from 1.1 in Q3’26, to 0.9 for Q4’26.

While a score of 0.9 sits firmly within the overweight range (defined as +0.5 to +1), cat bonds currently occupy joint second position among the manager’s conviction scores for Q4 2026. Technology leads the rankings with a score of 1.4, whereas fixed income, event-driven-special situations, and discretionary  share the second-place position, each registering a score of 0.9.

As mentioned, Franklin Templeton’s neutral stance on other insurance-linked securities (ILS) remains unchanged.

However, the manager’s conviction score for other ILS has moderately decreased from 0.4 in Q3’26, to -0.1 for Q4’26.

As we’ve alluded to before, many allocators still see a compelling investment case for catastrophe bonds, even following the recent price softening. While spreads have narrowed, attachment points and core terms and conditions have not meaningfully weakened for over three years now.

item.content:encoded:

Primary catastrophe bond market activity is set for a strong final quarter in 2026, driven by expectations for a strong pipeline and how the lower spread environment may encourage more sponsors to enter the market, according to Sidney Rostan, Head of ILS Strategies at SCOR Investment Partners.

SCOR Investment Partners is the asset management arm of the French reinsurance group and a specialist manager of insurance-linked securities (ILS) funds.

In a new commentary reflecting on the insurance-linked securities market’s performance in Q3 2026, Rostan highlighted that there were no meaningful insurance losses during the period, in what he described as “a very quiet US hurricane and Japan typhoon season, with no impactful landfall to be mentioned.”

“Like every year, the primary cat bond market became relatively quiet during the summer, with no transaction issued. This brings the YTD cat bond volume issued to approximately USD 18.5 billion as of the end of Q3 2026, slightly above volume issued during the same period in 2025,” Rostan said.

“In the absence of any threats in the tropical waters, the secondary cat bond market remained quiet during the summer, with only limited volumes traded. In this context, prices moved up significantly, driven by the customary seasonality effect which is at its strongest during the height of the hurricane/typhoon season.”

However, if we include the secondary market too, Artemis’ data shows that total catastrophe bond issuance for the first nine-months of the year set a new record of $18.9 billion.

Download your free copy of Artemis’ Q3 2026 Cat Bond & ILS Market Report here, where you can read more details, including a breakdown of deal flow by features such as perils, triggers, expected loss, and pricing, as well as analysis of the issuance trends seen by month and year.

Rostan further added: “In this environment, Q4 2026 is expected to see a very busy primary market according to discussions with cat bond structurers, as the lower spread environment will encourage potential cat bond sponsors to issue bonds in the context of a continuously increasing demand for protection.”

Given this, the executive underscored that total primary cat bond market activity could break last year’s full record of $25 billion.

Rostan also added that cat bond spreads are expected to come down slightly in the fourth quarter, emphasising that the high level of primary market issuances should sustain spread levels but should be well met given the level of capacity that’s currently available in the market.

Moving beyond the cat bond market, at both the June and July reinsurance renewals in the United States, rates continued their differentiated decline, with sharper reductions seen on quality cedents’ occurrence layers and more moderate decreases on aggregate and working layers, which resulted in a -15% to -20% risk-adjusted rate change YoY.

Following this year’s Rendez-Vous de Septembre in Monte Carlo, Rostan highlighted that well-capitalised markets are setting the stage for a shifting negotiation dynamic, pointing out that participants are expecting further, though more moderate softening in property catastrophe reinsurance pricing at the January renewals, and that negotiations are likely to extend beyond pricing, with terms and conditions as well as attachment levels expected to be key areas of focus during renewal discussions.

Lastly, Rostan also highlighted that the industry loss warranty (ILW) market remained quiet during Q3 2026 with no noticeable pricing changes seen during the period.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is actively promoting catastrophe bonds for sovereign disaster risk financing across the region, but Thomas Kessler noted last week that this will require cooperation across governments, research and modelling institutions, insurers and the ILS investor base.

Speaking in Bermuda at the Convergence 2026 conference last week, Thomas Kessler, Principal Disaster Risk Insurance & Finance Specialist at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) explained that replicating its first successful catastrophe bond issuances takes time and the engagement of insurance-linked securities market participants.

As we reported back in April 2026, the Asian Development Bank’s (ADB) first catastrophe bonds delivered $160 million of capital market-backed parametric earthquake and extreme precipitation disaster risk financing, evenly split between the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan.

These were the first transactions issued by the ADB’s own treasury facilities and proved the concept of issuing what it terms Disaster Relief Bonds (DRB), benefiting two of its members and securing them efficient disaster risk financing from institutional and insurance-linked securities (ILS) investors.

Importantly, Kessler explained that these catastrophe bonds come with a very clear mandate to deliver any payouts that are triggered during their coverage terms to provide social protection for specific groups.

This is not typical of catastrophe bonds, as they more frequently are used to provide reinsurance from the capital markets to insurer or reinsurer sponsors.

But in this case the Asian Development Bank designed the risk transfer to have a clear delivery of funding to groups expected to be most affected by the covered natural disaster events.

Kessler explained that the cat bonds were structured to have defined payout procedures, that aim to direct funds to vulnerable people and also provide investors with traceable impact reporting.

The parametric triggers themselves are designed to reflect affected populations, to ensure delivery of payout liquidity to support the recovery of those in the impacted regions who need it most.

As said, the payouts are designed to reach vulnerable households in the covered countries, with that delivered through existing national social protection systems, with the added benefit of reporting and auditing to support traceability for the investors that allocated to the bonds.

Kessler told the Convergence 2026 audience, “We actually set up SOPs, standard operating procedures, with many ministries in the countries. And we made sure that children, women, elderly people, people with disabilities, who are registered under the national social protection scheme, would benefit from the payouts, and we set in place reporting and auditing procedures in order to make sure that the household would get the money in case of a payout.”

This is an innovative way to both evidence the positive impact of any payout, while also ensuring it goes to those most in need of financial support when disaster strike.

It shows a way ILS structures can be designed to provide auditable impact, something that aligns well with the motivations of any sovereign sponsor and with many investors.

Kessler said, “This was highly appreciated by most of the investors, because it’s really the first time that we increased the transparency and the traceability of such an instrument, and we provided the investors with measurable SDG impact.

“Another unique feature is the triggers of these parametric bonds. So both earthquake and extreme precipitation were linked to the number of affected people, because they are eventually the beneficiary.”

Kessler also highlighted that the ADB created a web interface through which both the government’s and the investors could look at the modelling and monitor the impacts of perils, again an innovative feature of these cat bond deals.

Having completed its first catastrophe bond issuances, the ADB is now keen to replicate these deals and encourage other regional governments to look to disaster risk transfer as a valuable source of protection.

“ADB will further promote disaster relief bonds in Asia and the Pacific. We want to replicate them, take the momentum, and we’d like to have a regional approach,” Kessler explained.

“So we look at areas such as the Pacific Islands, which are faced with above average expected loss. We’re looking at Southeast Asia, the ASEAN, which combines large economies, further developed and also very small. We’re looking at the Hindu Kush Himalaya, you have seen the events in Nepal, Bhutan. And of course, we’re going to continue to work in in the CAREC region.

“So with this, we will provide opportunities for investors to diversify their portfolios geographically as well as into new risks, and we also hope that investors will get acquainted to new regions.”

Kessler closed by saying, “We can’t do it without cooperation between government, between academia, research institutions, science, modellers, structurers and the investors. MDBs, like the Asian Development Bank, can bring them all together.

“This leaves me with the saying: If you want to go fast you can go alone, but if you’re going to go far let’s go together, and let’s make an impact which is urgent.”

The severe convective storm and hail outbreak across parts of western Europe between August 26th and 28th 2026 is initially estimated to have caused nearly EUR 3.3 billion of insurance industry losses, according to catastrophe data aggregator PERILS AG.

This severe convective storm (SCS) outbreak that drove significant hail impacts affected parts of France, Germany, Switzerland and Italy from August 26th to 28th 2026, in an event also known as “SCS Raphaela”.

A number of large European insurance carriers have noted the potential for meaningful losses from this outbreak of severe and convective storms, with the hail damages particularly impactful and driving significant claims volumes. The event is seen as one of the largest catastrophe insured loss events to ever hit Switzerland, where the hail damage was extreme.

PERILS initially estimates the insurance market loss, based on data collected from affected insurers, at EUR 3,296 million, with those losses coming from the property and motor lines of business.

A cold front sweeping from west to east across France, Germany, Switzerland and Italy resulted in extensive SCS activity, driven by a low-pressure system named “Raphaela” by the Free University of Berlin, PERILS explained.

The storm system interacted with warm and humid air masses from the preceding heat waves across Europe, leading to the formation of numerous SCS systems including supercell storms that produced large hail, destructive winds and intense rainfall.

The loss event started in western France on August 26th, before impacting central and eastern France on August 27th, and Switzerland, southern Germany and northern Italy on August 28th.

PERILS explained that, “Hail ranging in size from 4-8 cm in diameter was reported in all countries. In France, the region of Besançon in the east was particularly badly affected. In Switzerland, a hail swath stretching from Lake Geneva in the west to Lake Constance in the northeast caused significant damage, as well as impacting southern Germany. In Italy, the northern regions of Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna were the most heavily affected, with hailstones of up to 13 cm in diameter recorded. The hailstorms were accompanied by very strong convective wind gusts and intense short-duration precipitation leading to flash flooding.

“There were no storm-related fatalities, but storm damage to property and cars was extensive. As a result, SCS Raphaela is one of the largest Cat losses on record for the Swiss insurance industry. For France, Italy and Germany, the industry losses were less exceptional and remained below the extreme levels experienced in recent years.”

Luzi Hitz, Product Manager at PERILS, added, “The Raphaela storms are the second SCS event in Europe in 2026 exceeding EUR 2bn in industry losses. Like the event in mid-July, they originated out of the preceding heatwave which provided ample thermal energy and humidity to support SCS formation. Both events underscore the destructive potential of European summer weather transitions. A primary contributing factor is the ever-warming atmosphere which generates increasing levels of ‘fuel’ for severe convective storms. As the climate looks unlikely to cool in the foreseeable future, the potential exists for multi-billion SCS events in Europe to become the new normal.”

Hannover Re’s property and casualty reinsurance subsidiary in Germany anticipates continued strong reinsurance demand at the next rounds of renewals, but notes that rising capacity levels are driving more competition on pricing and terms, while also highlighting insurance-linked securities (ILS) as a complementary offering for clients.

With the Baden-Baden reinsurance meetings underway in the country, Hannover Re’s German subsidiary has given its outlook for the regional marketplace, explaining that risks are rising despite moderate catastrophe loss costs of late.

Competition is intensifying in many parts of the reinsurance market in the region, as traditional players have growing capital bases.

But overall, the company believes demand for high-quality reinsurance protection will remain strong in Germany, with a stable environment overall but characterised by an increasing level of competition to deploy capacity.

Thorsten Steinmann, Chief Executive Officer of E+S Rück and the member of Hannover Re’s Executive Board responsible for property and casualty reinsurance in Continental Europe, Latin America and North Africa commented, “The moderate catastrophe losses of the past few years should not obscure what remains a demanding and highly uncertain risk landscape. Natural perils, inflation, cyber risks and geopolitical instabilities are adding to the potential for losses and confronting insurers and reinsurers alike with increasingly complex challenges.

“At the same time, many primary insurers have significantly strengthened their earnings and capital position. This builds stability and establishes a good foundation for the upcoming renewals. With certain segments becoming increasingly competitive, we continue to view a disciplined underwriting policy as well as risk-adequate prices and conditions as essential for ensuring the long-term availability and viability of reinsurance protection.”

Inflation and costs continue to rise in P&C reinsurance and in clients natural catastrophe reinsurance programmes E+S Rück still sees many of them “adequately priced to reflect the risks.”

But rising capacity, thanks to higher capital bases of traditional companies, is “leading to more intense competition and adding to the pressure on prices and conditions.”

Recent catastrophe losses from hail events in Switzerland, southern Germany, northern Italy and the neighbouring Alpine regions demonstrate that the underlying risks remain high, the Hannover Re subsidiary said.

“In the upcoming renewals, therefore, the individual claims experience, the quality of the programmes as well as risk-appropriate prices and conditions will continue to be decisive factors for E+S Rück,” the company explained this morning.

Catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities (ILS) offer alternative and increasingly important capacity solutions.

E+S Rück explained, “Alternative risk transfer solutions continue to gain in importance. Insurance-linked securities (ILS) complement traditional reinsurance by providing additional capital market capacity.

“In cooperation with Hannover Re, E+S Rück offers its clients access to ILS solutions.”

Here are the ten most popular news articles, week ending October 18th 2026, covering catastrophe bonds, ILS, reinsurance capital and related risk transfer topics. To ensure you never miss a thing subscribe to the weekly Artemis email newsletter updates or get our email alerts for every article we publish.


Ten most read articles on Artemis.bm, week ending October 18th 2026:

  1. Hurricane Simon track remained outside of Mexico cat bond parametric trigger zones: Loconte
    As major hurricane Simon’s path shifted west it remained offshore of the parametric trigger zones related to the $175 million IBRD CAR Mexico 2024 (Pacific) catastrophe bond, according to analysis by Isacco Loconte, an ILS Investment Specialist at asset manager Azimut Switzerland SA.
  2. Pillar Capital Management gets strategic investment from SageSure
    Pillar Capital Management, the Bermuda-based specialist collateralized reinsurance and insurance-linked securities investment fund manager, has secured a new high-profile backer as managing general underwriter SageSure has made a strategic investment in the company.
  3. 777 co-founder Wander pleads guilty to $500m+ scheme to defraud lenders and investors
    Josh Wander, one of the co-founders of investment firm 777 Partners, has pled guilty to wire fraud and securities fraud in connection with a $500 million plus scheme to defraud lenders and investors of the company.
  4. Hurricane Isaias insurance industry loss estimated in $2bn – $4bn range: Euler ILS Partners
    Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, has placed an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion, noting there is the potential for the storm’s losses to add to aggregate structures.
  5. Swiss Re says increased reinsurance supply a positive, will align alt capital where it makes sense
    Speaking ahead of the 2026 Baden-Baden gathering, Leopoldo Camara, Head of P&C Reinsurance Northern, Central & Eastern Europe at Swiss Re outlined that more reinsurance capital is needed in the market to address growing, interconnected risks, while also emphasising that the reinsurer will use its deep risk expertise to align alternative capital where it makes sense.
  6. KCC estimates hurricane Isaias wind and surge insured losses at $3bn
    Karen Clark & Company (KCC) has provided an initial estimate for the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias, saying it expects the total to be $3 billion.
  7. Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures
    As industry focus grows on designing efficient structures to enable capital to connect with reinsurance risk, Lloyd’s has issued guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures, which is a strategy that Lloyd’s itself believes is likely to see increasing demand.
  8. PICC P&C’s new $12m Great Wall Re is the first Hong Kong sidecar ILS issuance
    PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited has now reported that its new US $12 million issuance of insurance-linked securities under Great Wall Re Limited is actually a quota share reinsurance sidecar, the first in Hong Kong, designed to provide protection to its offshore wind power property insurance book on the Chinese Mainland.
  9. Evolving captives becoming strategic platforms for attracting third-party capital: Aon
    Captives are rapidly evolving from risk retention vehicles into strategic capital access platforms, which in turn is beginning to attract third-party capital, according to broker Aon, who emphasises that captive owners are increasingly partnering with external investors to unlock capacity that supports growth initiatives and long-term resilience.
  10. ILS investors need to speak up and ask for alternative model views: Karen Clark
    At the ILS Bermuda Convergence 2026 conference, Karen Clark, CEO and Co-founder of catastrophe risk modelling specialist Karen Clark & Company, urged the insurance-linked securities community and its investors to ask for alternative model views to be included in the deal flow that comes to market.

This is not every article published on Artemis during the last week, just the most popular among our readers over the last seven days. There were 33 new articles published in the last week.

Global re/insurer Generali is the latest to enter the Lloyd’s market with what seems a sidecar-like syndicate as a way to enhance and make its reinsurance arrangements more efficient, while the announcements points to the potential for alternative and capital markets to be involved.

Generali said today it is entering Lloyd’s with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, for which it has now received in-principle approval to begin underwriting operations on the Lloyd’s platform in 2027.

The insurer said this move is “a significant step forward in the Group’s reinsurance strategy, enhancing access to diversified sources of risk capital while reinforcing long-term partnerships across the global reinsurance market.”

Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge will assume a share of Generali’s outward reinsurance placements, across multiple lines of business.

As such this seems the latest example of a sidecar-style syndicate at Lloyd’s for a major re/insurance group.

In addition, Generali said that its entry to Lloyd’s brings “a distinctive diversification opportunity” given the insurer’s geographical footprint and type of ceded businesses.

Generali’s outward reinsurance portfolio offers significant exposure to continental European risks, the company explained, which it sees as a complement to Lloyd’s more traditional global focus. It also provides a balanced mix of retail and middle market business access across multiple classes and territories.

Franco Urlini, Group P&C & Reinsurance Officer of Generali, explained, “The launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge marks an important milestone in the evolution of our reinsurance strategy under the “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” plan, with the goal to optimise capital at Group level. By leveraging the Lloyd’s global platform, we can develop tailored and innovative risk transfer solutions while accessing new sources of capital to support the growth ambitions of our P&C portfolio. It is an extension of our strategy aimed at maintaining broad and diversified access to reinsurance and alternative capital markets while adding a further tool to the Group’s risk transfer capabilities.”

Note Urlini’s mention of accessing “new sources of capital” while also citing Generali’s strategy to diversify sources using alternative capital markets.

Dawn Miller, Chief Commercial Officer of Lloyd’s and CEO of Lloyd’s Americas, added, “Our ambition is to attract the leading global underwriters to Lloyd’s, so we are delighted to be welcoming Generali with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge. This vehicle will open up deeper connections between insurance, reinsurance and capital markets, underscoring Lloyd’s role as the leading global marketplace for innovative risk transfer solutions.”

Note there, that Miller mentioned that Generali’s syndicate will deepen connections to capital markets as well.

The commentary suggests that there may be a plan to bring in capital market backers to the syndicate, as a result it’s also possible that Lloyd’s insurance-linked securities (ILS) structure might be used, the London Bridge 2 PCC vehicle.

It’s important to add that at this stage, no clarity has been given as to the backers of Generali’s syndicate, whether there is outside capital in from the start, or the insurer is funding it, or how capital will be channelled.

But, given the strategy of ceding a portion of its outwards reinsurance placement to the syndicate, it perhaps suggests there might be more direct participation from other capital providers. As we said though, that is not immediately made clear from the announcement.

The use of the Lloyd’s platform to set up sidecar style reinsurance syndicates, to optimise and enhance reinsurance programmes and capital usage, is a growing trend, often involving the London Bridge platform.

In the last year we’ve seen Blackstone partner with The Fidelis Partnership on Syndicate 2126, while the same asset manager partnered with AIG on Syndicate 2479, which was that insurer’s second such vehicle after the also Blackstone-partnered Syndicate 2478.

Apollo has been selected as the managing agent for this new syndicate.

Reinsurance brokerage Howden Re, acted as Generali’s exclusive adviser on the transaction, working across Howden Re International, Howden Re Capital Solutions and Howden Capital Markets & Advisory.

Massimo Reina, CEO, Howden Re International, said, “This transaction demonstrates the value of combining deep insurance sector expertise with a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working as one team across Howden, we have supported Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and attract third-party support from across the Lloyd’s capital ecosystem. Interest in the opportunity reflects the continued appeal of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

Vijay Mavani, Managing Director, Howden Capital Solutions, added, “This transaction demonstrates the value of the integrated Howden platform, combining deep reinsurance expertise, capital solutions capabilities and a strong understanding of Lloyd’s capital. Working closely with Philipp Kusche and colleagues across Howden Capital Markets & Advisory, we have operated as one team to support Generali in creating a tailored platform designed to broaden its strategic options and facilitate access to capital from across the Lloyd’s ecosystem. The level of interest in the opportunity highlights the continued attractiveness of the Lloyd’s market to a diverse range of capital providers.”

Also read from earlier today: Lloyd’s issues guidance and expectations for broker-originated reinsurance structures.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

As industry focus grows on designing efficient structures to enable capital to connect with reinsurance risk, Lloyd’s has issued guidance on its expectations for any broker-originated reinsurance structures, which is a strategy that Lloyd’s itself believes is likely to see increasing demand.

The issue of this guidance note from Lloyd’s comes on the heels of the high-profile news around Aon’s partnership with Blackstone on the vehicle widely said to be codenamed Cortina.

That strategy sees Aon looking to bring Blackstone into Lloyd’s, to support a share of the business it brokers in the market, which represents another signal of capital market and asset manager appetite to gain access to broadly diversified insurance and reinsurance market returns.

Lloyd’s framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures provides market guidance as to the approach, its expectations and what the approval requirements will be for broker-originated reinsurance structures.

The Aon – Blackstone news raised many questions, so this appears to be at least in part a response to that, to place some clarity around what Lloyd’s will tolerate and expect from those seeking to replicate, or design different structures to achieve similar outcomes (the outcomes being new capital entrants backing meaningful portfolios of risk underwritten there).

Third-party capital’s appetite to access returns from the reinsurance market in general and business from Lloyd’s has risen fast in the last couple of years.

At the same time, new structures and strategies are making it possible to bring capital market participants more deeply into the Lloyd’s market, in support of syndicates, so-called ReShares and broker facilities. In addition, the London Bridge structures have also provided more efficient mechanisms for routing third-party capital into the market’s underwriting workflow.

Lloyd’s explained in a market bulletin issued by Rachel Turk, Chief of Performance and Strategy, “The growth of broker facilities and third-party capital solutions has created an emerging opportunity for broker-led reinsurance portfolios supported by external capital. We expect demand for these structures to increase.

“We have today issued a clear framework for how these structures are overseen at Lloyd’s that will take effect from 1st January 2027. The framework is transparent, principles-based, and provides the market with clarity on Lloyd’s appetite, expectations and guardrails for such structures.

“The new framework seeks to support innovation and growth while maintaining underwriting discipline and protecting the Central Fund. It is anchored around Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target and establishes clear requirements relating to market concentration, ownership and capital, governance, managing agent capabilities,
underwriting guardrails, portfolio oversight and eligibility criteria.

“Consistent with Lloyd’s broader approach, broker-originated reinsurance structures are subject to the standard new entrant approval process and ongoing oversight arrangements.”

Facilities have existed at Lloyd’s for many years, including broker run facility structures.

But, in the past these have tended to have multiple markets backing them, largely traditional insurance and reinsurance players. Where as now, we see asset managers and capital markets players having facilities-of-one, of sorts, as they seek to derive exposure to an index, or index of a sub-set of the Lloyd’s markets underwriting business and returns.

As a strategy, it makes perfect sense, in delivering large-scale access to a broad and diversified swathe of risk. But for Lloyd’s, there is the rest of the market and its participants to consider, hence the issuance of guidelines to help the market understand what will be allowed and tolerated.

Lloyd’s has explained some of the features of its framework for broker-originated reinsurance structures in the market.

Any such venture will need to show its alignment with Lloyd’s cross-cycle 95% net combined operating ratio target, while they will initially be curtailed to a market-wide risk appetite of up to 10% of an individual broker’s treaty portfolio that can be placed into these structures.

In addition, Lloyd’s said that brokers cannot own or capitalise these reinsurance structures themselves. Of course, that would be a step too far over the boundary between broker and underwriter.

There has to be a minimum capital participation requirement from the member aligned to the managing agent of 19.99%, while at least 25% of capacity must be provided by the lead reinsurers, with the panel agreed by the managing agent.

Some business is considered out of scope for broker-originated reinsurance structures in Lloyd’s, including hybrid fronting carriers, MGUs and legacy providers, captive involvement needs a prior submit arrangement and there can be no exposure to Cyber war “type 4” language.

Interestingly, Lloyd’s also seems to want to see a commitment from those participating as cedents, saying, “Once the participation cede has been determined as part of the overall proposition, cedents must cede either all of their eligible portfolio with the respective broker to the structure, or none of it.”

While the managing agent must be sophisticated enough, in terms of reinsurance analysis and pricing, to challenge the assumptions provided by the broker.

Reporting and oversight will be key, with regular engagement with Lloyd’s and data sharing, as well as agreed guardrails needing to be in place that the capital provider and managing agent must contractually agree on.

Importantly, Lloyd’s does not want these structures running unfettered, saying, “If indexation of at least 70% has not been reached by year 3 of the structure, Lloyd’s and the managing agent will agree next steps which can include winding up the structure.”

Annual plans and any mid-year changes will need to be approved, as they are for other more traditional Lloyd’s underwriting structures. While standard new entrant capital allocation rules and timings will apply.

Finally and perhaps the most important guideline, efficiencies generated by the broker-originated reinsurance strategy must find their way back to the protection buyers.

Lloyd’s will expect the cedent to share in the efficiencies generated by the structure (both operational and capital) through the mechanism of a client dividend, the market explained.

Lloyd’s stated, “The framework applies to all broker-originated reinsurance structures seeking approval to operate within Lloyd’s and should be considered alongside the standard new entrant approval process.”

Alternative, third-party and capital markets investors are extremely interested in efficient ways to gain access to insurance and reinsurance risks at this time and over recent years Lloyd’s has itself shown that it is increasingly open to seeing new capital enter the market in more efficient ways.

It’s important to have some guidelines around it, so it’s good to see the market responding and issuing this bulletin.

However, it does raise one question. How many similar strategies of meaningful scale, backed by large capital market players (the Blackstone types), could and should Lloyd’s allow, without risking upsetting the broader market’s sentiment and equilibrium?

Of course, if efficient capital can be put to work to bring much more underwriting business into Lloyd’s that is a good thing, as long as discipline and prudence are observed.

But we all know what too much capital can do and there is a perhaps-challenging balancing-act to be followed, to keep the established market participants on-side as Lloyd’s itself evolves and broker’s increasingly marshal capital more directly to risk.

item.content:encoded:
This content is copyright to www.artemis.bm and should not appear anywhere else, or an infringement has occurred.

Moody’s RMS Event Response has now provided an initial estimate of insurance industry losses from recent hurricane Isaias, placing them in a range between $2.5 billion and $4.5 billion.

Moody’s said that its best estimate is $3.5 billion, as you might expect the mid-point of the range and that the estimate represents insured losses from wind, storm surge, and precipitation-induced flooding damages.

Wind damage is the majority of the losses from hurricane Isaias, Moody’s explained, while storm surge, precipitation-induced inland flooding, and the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) losses are expected to be only around $250 million of the total.

Moody’s estimate includes insured property damage and business interruption for residential, commercial, industrial, automobile, as well as watercraft lines of business, and it also accounts for sources of post-event loss amplification (PLA).

We can compare Moody’s estimate to others, such as the most recent from Karen Clark & Company (KCC) that estimated the private insurance market loss from wind and storm surge associated with recent hurricane Isaias would be $3 billion.

Verisk gave its initial industry insured loss estimate for Isaias recently, saying that onshore property losses from the storm could reach $2 billion.

In addition, Euler ILS Partners, the specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities (ILS) investment manager, put an initial insurance industry loss estimate for recent hurricane Isaias in the range of $2 billion to $4 billion.

Cotality (formerly CoreLogic), estimated that insured losses from wind and storm surge from hurricane Isaias will be in the $2 billion to $3 billion range, while Gallagher Re said industry losses will fall in the lower end of the low to mid-single-digit billions of dollars range and AM Best said insured loss estimates are expected to be in the low single digit range in billions of dollars.

Moody’s estimate is one of the higher, but still all the estimates top-out at $4.5 billion in range terms, at which level hurricane Isaias is not expected to be a significant reinsurance event, aside from perhaps a few very low layers and any quota share reinsurance participations that are exposed.

Jeff Waters, Director – North Atlantic Hurricane Models, Moody’s, commented: “Hurricane Isaias was yet another example of a storm that intensified quickly over the anomalously warm ocean waters in the Gulf, a region that usually sees higher hurricane activity during El Niño years. Thankfully, the storm encountered strong wind shear as it approached landfall, which disrupted its structure and weakened the wind field considerably. As a result, we expect the overall extent and severity of insured losses from this event to be manageable for the market.”

Raj Vojjala, Managing Director – Modeling and Analytics, Moody’s, said, “Many exposures impacted by Hurricane Isaias were also impacted by recent storms like Hurricanes Sally and Zeta in 2020, and Helene in 2024, which led to widespread roof repairs and replacements. We expect these efforts to have improved the risk profile and structural resilience of the region’s building stock to hurricane winds, especially for an event like Isaias. Nevertheless, a high incidence of treefall-driven roof damage in the affected area and potential roof replacements due to Florida’s 25% roof rule, which can require full replacement of certain roofs when repairs exceed a specified threshold, will drive insured losses in this event.”
